transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-14
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Marco Ruiz (Redwood SE), Aisha Rahman (QuantumForge Head of Platform), Tom Erickson (NetOps), Priya Gopal (Security), Benjy Cole (SRE)

Auto-generated summary (short):
Customer evaluating Redwood Private for multi-region inference with strict data residency and on-prem burst; primary questions around private endpoints, transit gateway vs. peering, egress inspection, and KMS/HSM integration.

Topics: private endpoints, VPC peering, Transit Gateway, AWS PrivateLink vs. peering, region gating, on-prem burst VPNs, encryption/KMS, SOC2/security artifacts, latency budgets.

--- Transcript body ---
[00:00] Lena (Redwood AE): All right good afternoon everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call so I know who we have — I'm Lena, AE on the account, Marco from our SE org is here.
[00:14] Aisha (QuantumForge): Hi all, Aisha here. Tom and Priya and Benjy are on from platform and security.
[00:20] Marco (Redwood SE): Hey folks, Marco, happy to dig in on networking. I know QuantumForge has some interesting multi-region constraints so let's just get high level first.
[00:28] Tom (QuantumForge - NetOps): Yeah, thanks. To frame it — we have GDPR plus a German subsidiary that requires data to stay in eu-central-1 for certain customers. Also occasional on-prem bursts for inference (rare but non-zero), so we're evaluating private options.
[00:42] Lena: Great. The usual three modes we talk about are hosted API, dedicated capacity, and private VPC deployments. Today sounds like Private is front and center, correct?
[00:52] Aisha: Yes, Private or Dedicated with VPC peering — we need isolation, and a strong egress story.
[01:00] Marco: Cool. Two quick clarifying q's — 1) Which clouds/regions do you need Redwood to be present in? And 2) Do you prefer PrivateLink/Private Endpoint or VPC peering/transit gateway?
[01:12] Priya (Security): For us priority regions are eu-central-1, eu-west-1, and us-east-1. For some customers we also need APAC, but that's lower priority. On connectivity, default preference is PrivateLink, but if latency is too high we might consider Transit Gateway or direct peering.
[01:28] Benjy (SRE): Also want to call out that our corporate network does deep packet inspection at the egress layer so egress posture matter — ability to present fixed IPs and have mutual TLS with HSM-backed certs is required for prod.
[01:40] Lena: Good intel — the fixed IP and mTLS bit is super common. We can support static egress IPs from Redwood Private nodes per region and we integrate with customer KMS for key wrapping — Marco can fill in specifics.
[01:53] Marco: Yep, we have KMS integrations (customer-managed keys) and can support HSM-backed keys for token encryption and audit logging. One nuance: in some configs we terminate TLS at the inference host inside the customer's VPC via PrivateLink — that reduces egress scanning surface but requires PrivateLink endpoint setup.
[02:14] Tom: When you say terminate TLS inside our VPC via PrivateLink — do you mean the Redwood host has an ENI inside our VPC?
[02:22] Marco: Exactly. For AWS PrivateLink we create an interface endpoint in your VPC and the traffic stays in-pla- — (pause) sorry — stays in the AWS network, it doesn't hairpin out to public internet. That gives you an ENI, private IPs, and we can advertise a stable DN/ips for your firewall.
[02:40] Tom: Ok that matches our preference. But we also need to think about multi-region routing — some customers in Germany must never leave eu-central-1. How do you support pinning model endpoints by region?
[02:54] Lena: We expose model versions with region affinity. For Private we can pin deployments to specific regions and set routing policies so requests from eu-central-1 hit eu-central-1 nodes. We also support automated fallback but that can be disabled for strict residency.
[03:08] Aisha: Fallback disabled is a requirement for certain SLAs. If eu-central-1 capacity is exhausted we want requests to fail rather than route to us-east-1. Is that doable?
[03:18] Marco: Yes — you can configure strict locality. One gotcha: there is an availability cost — if you want both strict residency and high availability you need dedicated capacity in-region or reserved nodes. That's part of the dedicated vs private tradeoff.
[03:32] Benjy: Can you clarify dedicated vs private here? We thought Dedicated = reserved GPU pool managed by Redwood in your account and Private = you host in our VPC.
[03:41] Lena: Slightly different wording across vendors causes confusion. Our terminology: Dedicated is reserved capacity hosted by Redwood in our tenancy but isolated for you — good for predictable throughput and lower ops. Private is our private deployment option where a Redwood control plane manages nodes that are provisioned in your VPC (or on-prem). In Private the network boundary is fully yours.
[03:59] Priya: Important for us — will Redwood have access to logs in Private? We need to ensure separation and audit.
[04:06] Marco: By default, audit logs can be streamed to your S3 / CloudWatch / Event Hub. We also support a private control plane mode where logs are only in your account and Redwood's support access is through just-in-time support sessions. We can disable some telemetry if needed.
[04:22] Tom: About IPs — can you provide a short list of egress IP ranges per region? Our firewall team needs it for allowlisting.
[04:30] Lena: Yes, we'll provide an egress IP matrix. For Private deployments the egress IPs will be under your VPC NAT/gateway so it's typically under your control, but for Dedicated/hosted we provide a published list per region.
[04:44] Aisha: For on-prem bursts we plan to tunnel via our VPN to a cloud halo then route to the inference nodes — is that supported?
[04:54] Marco: We support VPN and direct connect peering into the VPCs. For bursts we recommend a Transit Gateway + route tables approach to avoid hairpin complexity.
[05:04] Benjy: Any constraints on MTU or packet inspection? Our VPN vendors sometimes do weird fragmentation and we don't want the KV cache traffic to break.
[05:12] Marco: Good point — we recommend MTU 1500 and avoid jumbo frames unless you control the full path. For KV cache traffic (we heard kv cache but transcript mis- says 'kay vee') small messages are fine. We'll share an ops checklist with MTU/keepalive settings.
[05:28] [Speaker 1]: (crosstalk)
[05:32] Tom: Security — SAML SSO for console and RBAC for tokens — what are options?
[05:37] Lena: We support SAML/SSO for console and RBAC controls. For token issuance we can integrate with your identity provider for short-lived tokens. We also support SCIM provisioning.
[05:47] Priya: Audit trails — retention and forensic access?
[05:51] Marco: Audit logs can be retained in your storage; we also produce structured request logs. Retention is configurable and for Private you control the retention policy.
[06:00] Aisha: One operational question — who manages cert rotation for PrivateLink ENIs?
[06:05] Marco: Typically the customer owns the endpoint certs — we can support mutual TLS with certs issued by your CA or we can use ACM with customer-managed keys. For HSM-backed workflows we reference an HSM integration for signing.
[06:20] Lena: Ok shifting to perf — what's your latency SLO for inference?
[06:25] Benjy: Target is 80th percentile under 150ms for single-turn smallish prompts (256 tokens). For longer chat sessions we have different SLAs.
[06:34] Marco: Rough sketch — if you colocate in-region via PrivateLink you should see ~20-60ms p50 depending on instance type for small prompts. Cross-region (eu-central to us-west) will add more, obviously. We'll run quick numbers and share.
[06:50] Tom: Another point — egress inspection team will want to man-in-the-middle TLS for inspection. Does that break signature verification and how do we support that?
[06:59] Priya: Yes, we do TLS intercept for outbound to public endpoints for some customers — for Private we hope to avoid that.
[07:05] Marco: If you're doing TLS intercept inside your corporate network it can break end-to-end mTLS. Our recommendation is to use PrivateLink so traffic doesn't cross public egress points and you can reduce interception. If you must intercept, we can use mTLS with client certs issued by your CA inside the VPC so the inspection still sees plaintext — but that is obviously a security tradeoff.
[07:26] Aisha: Understood.
[07:30] [00:07:30] Lena: Quick pause — any legal/procurement constraints?
[07:35] Aisha: We'll need standard DPAs and some additional clauses for German data residency. Procurement will also want a runbook for incident response.
[07:43] Lena: We'll attach our DPA and incident runbook.
[07:46] Tom: One more — egress bandwidth estimates. If we ramp to 10k qps what egress do you expect?
[07:53] Marco: That depends heavily on token volume. We'll ask for typical prompt size and RPS and produce a bandwidth estimate — we can simulate with a small load generator.
[08:03] Benjy: Could you run a spike test from eu-central to an on-prem endpoint?
[08:07] Marco: Yes, we can do a POC where we spin up a private deployment in eu-central-1 within your VPC and run spike tests. We usually do a two-week POC.
[08:17] Aisha: Budget/timeline question — how fast can we get a Private deployment in eu-central? We need something minimal for a POC in 2-3 weeks.
[08:25] Lena: If procurement is okay and you sign an initial PO for a pilot, we can stand up a small Private cluster in about 7–10 business days. Provisioning depends on access to the VPC and subnet allocations.
[08:36] Priya: We will need to do a security review before production — will Redwood join a security interview?
[08:42] Lena: Absolutely — we have a security team that does SOC2 walk-throughs. I'll coordinate.
[08:47] [00:08:47] Tom: Are there any limitations with Azure/GCP? We primarily run on AWS but a subset of customers are GCP.
[08:56] Marco: We support Azure and GCP for Private deployments; there are slight differences in PrivateLink (Azure Private Endpoint) naming and in how we handle peering. We'll share the cloud-specific checklist.
[09:07] Benjy: KMS integration — we use Google Cloud KMS for the GCP tenants, and AWS KMS for AWS. Is that supported?
[09:14] Marco: Yes, we have cloud-native KMS integrations and you can bring your own keys in each region. For cross-region key usage there are constraints; best practice is to keep keys in-region.
[09:25] Aisha: Anything else on the networking front we should be aware of?
[09:29] Marco: A couple items: 1) NAT vs. EIP design — prefer EIPs for stable allowlists if you control them; 2) Route table design for Transit Gateway to avoid asymmetric routing; 3) Healthchecks and probe ports — we'll require a small set of ports opened for control plane and metrics scraping. We'll send the exact port list.
[09:48] Tom: If the customer wants full air-gap/on-prem, how deep does Redwood go?
[09:54] Lena: We have an on-prem package that can be air-gapped — it's heavier and requires more ops on your side. That option typically involves us delivering a software bundle and running an initial onboarding with your ops team. We can do that for regulated customers but it's a different commercial model.
[10:08] [00:10:08] Priya: Regarding auditability — can we sign an NDA for deeper log sharing for the security review?
[10:13] Lena: Yes, we can sign an NDA.
[10:15] Aisha: Ok next steps for us — we'll compile a list of required regions, provide our sample RPS and prompt sizes, and decide whether we prefer PrivateLink-first or Transit Gateway.
[10:25] Lena: Great. Recap from Redwood side: we'll send security artifacts (SOC2/ISO), Private deployment architecture + port/IP matrix, a rough latency sketch for eu-central-local vs cross-region, and a proposed POC plan with timeline.
[10:40] Marco: I will also prepare a brief runbook for the spike test and a perf script.
[10:45] Benjy: Sounds good.
[10:47] [00:10:47] (crosstalk)
[10:50] Aisha: Any blockers to scheduling the POC kickoff?
[10:53] Lena: Procurement and access to the VPC subnets are the main ones. If you can give us a sandbox VPC and role we can start.
[10:58] Tom: We can provide a sandbox VPC. I'll follow up with the subnet ranges.
[11:03] Lena: Perfect. Thanks everyone. We'll follow up in email with the artifacts.
[11:07] Aisha: Thanks — appreciate it.
[11:10] Marco: Cheers.
[11:12] Lena: End call.

End of transcript.
